title: Trailing coloured slip on wet clay
subtitle: Applying slip lines and dots in flowing patterns on a fresh clay surface
excerpt: Slip trailing is the technique of applying liquid clay (slip) through a narrow nozzle onto a fresh clay surface to draw lines, dots, and patterns. On air-dry clay, the slip bonds as it dries and creates a raised-line decoration. Traditional English slipware used this method on earthenware; this tutorial adapts it for air-dry clay with no kiln required.
sourceNotes: Slip-trailing technique derived from traditional English slipware practice documented from the seventeenth century onward. Air-dry adaptation derived from contemporary no-kiln craft methodology.

glossaryTerms.definition: Clay diluted with water to a brushable or pourable consistency, used for surface decoration and joining.
The drying stage where clay holds its shape: the correct moisture level for slip trailing on the clay body.
Earthenware or stoneware decorated with slip, usually trailed or dipped, before firing. A major tradition in British studio pottery from the seventeenth century.

content.text: Traditional
slipware
was made in Staffordshire, Devon, and Sussex from the 1600s to the 1800s. Potters trailed liquid
slip
through a goose quill onto fresh clay. The lines stood up from the surface and survived firing. The same technique works on air-dry clay. The
slip
bonds to the fresh clay as both dry. The raised lines are sealed over at the end.

The tool is a slip trailer: a small rubber bulb with a nozzle, available from pottery suppliers. An alternative is a small squeezy bottle with a fine nozzle (a food-decoration bottle works well). The nozzle diameter determines the width of the trailed line.
What you need
Fresh or
leather-hard

air-dry clay slab or formed piece. Coloured slip: either commercial coloured-slip-white or coloured-slip-black, or homemade (air-dry clay dissolved in water with acrylic paint added for colour). A slip trailer or small squeezy bottle with a 2 to 3 mm nozzle.
Preparing the slip

The slip must flow smoothly through the nozzle without running or dripping uncontrolled. The right consistency is slightly thicker than single cream: it falls in a slow, continuous thread from the nozzle when the bulb or bottle is tilted but does not drip on its own.

Test the flow on a piece of card before touching the clay. If the slip blobs rather than threads, thin with a few drops of water. If it spreads flat immediately, thicken by leaving it uncovered for 10 minutes to thicken through evaporation.
Trailing the design

Lay the clay slab flat or use a banding wheel for round pieces. The clay should be at leather-hard: firm enough to hold the trailed slip without absorbing it into the surface, fresh enough for the slip to bond as it dries.

Hold the nozzle 5 to 10 mm above the clay surface. Apply steady pressure to the bulb and move the nozzle at a consistent speed: too slow and the slip builds up too thick; too fast and the thread breaks. The thread of slip should sit up slightly above the clay surface rather than sinking in.

For traditional slipware patterns: parallel wavy lines across the piece, or a spiral from centre to rim, or a simple lettering. Let the first colour dry slightly before adding a second colour in a cross-pattern or dots.

For feathering (a classic slipware effect): trail parallel lines of two alternating colours across the slab. While still wet, draw a needle tool or comb across the lines at right angles to produce a feather or herringbone pattern.
Allow the trailed design to dry with the piece. Do not attempt to move the piece until the slip is at least leather-hard: the trailed lines are fragile while wet and will smear if the piece is moved.
Common mistakes
Slip sinks into the clay surface and loses the raised line: clay too wet; slip too thin. Use leather-hard clay and thicken the slip.
Thread breaks mid-line: air bubble in the slip; nozzle clogged. Purge the nozzle with a burst of pressure on scrap card before continuing.
Slip thread curls rather than trailing straight: nozzle held too high above surface; slip too thick. Lower the nozzle closer to the clay and thin the slip very slightly.

rows.problem: Trailed lines crack when the piece dries
rows.cause: Slip and clay body shrinking at different rates
rows.fix: Use slip made from the same clay body as the piece. Commercial coloured slip matched to the clay body's shrinkage reduces cracking.

rows.problem: Feathering smears rather than drawing clean chevrons
rows.cause: Needle tool pulled when slip too wet; lines too far apart
rows.fix: Allow the trailed lines to stiffen for 2 to 3 minutes before feathering. Space parallel lines no more than 5 mm apart.
